title: The last supper (Luke 22:14–20)
hook: bread broken, a cup shared, and "do this in remembrance of me"

segments.voice: Yesterday, a teacher with a towel, kneeling at his friends' feet. Today, the same night, the meal itself.

A meal you'll never forget. Maybe the last dinner with someone before they moved away, or before they died. You didn't know it was the last one, or maybe you did. You remember where everyone sat. Now, an upstairs room in Jerusalem at Passover, the feast when Jewish families remember how God brought their ancestors out of slavery in Egypt, with bread and wine and the old story told again. Jesus sits down with his friends. And he knows this is the last time.
screen: `A MEAL YOU'LL NEVER FORGET.` → `AN UPSTAIRS ROOM AT PASSOVER.` → `HE KNOWS IT'S THE LAST TIME.`

segments.voice: Luke gives his first words at the table, in the King James Bible: "With desire I have desired to eat this passover with you before I suffer." That doubling is a Hebrew way of saying, I have longed and longed for this. Then he does what the head of the table did at a Jewish meal: takes bread, gives thanks, breaks it, and hands it around. But then he says something no one had heard at Passover before: "This is my body which is given for you: this do in remembrance of me." And after supper, the cup: "This cup is the new testament in my blood, which is shed for you." Testament here means covenant, a binding promise between God and people, like the one made with Israel at Sinai. The big word is remembrance; in Greek, anamnesis. It means more than recalling a fact. At Passover, Jewish families speak as if they themselves came out of Egypt; the past becomes present at the table. Christians have shared this meal ever since, and understand it differently. Catholics and Orthodox Christians believe the bread and wine truly become Christ's body and blood. Lutherans speak of Christ truly present in, with and under the bread and wine. Many Reformed Christians speak of a real spiritual presence. Many Baptists and others see it as a memorial, a powerful act of remembering. The names differ too: the Eucharist, from the Greek for gave thanks; Holy Communion; the Lord's Supper; the Mass; the Divine Liturgy. What almost all of them share is the table, the bread, the cup, and his words: do this, and remember me.
screen: `WITH DESIRE I HAVE DESIRED.` · `BREAD TAKEN, BLESSED, BROKEN, GIVEN.` · `A NEW COVENANT IN A CUP.` · `ANAMNESIS: THE PAST MADE PRESENT.` · then, large: `THIS DO IN REMEMBRANCE OF ME.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you'd like to remember at your next meal: someone who's gone, or far away, or who taught you something at a table. What did they eat, what did they say, where did they sit? Let them come close, and picture that meal eaten slowly, no screen, with them in mind; if you pray, you can give thanks before the first bite.
Anamnesis. The Greek word for remembrance, calling the past into the present, which is what Jesus asked his friends to do with the bread and the cup.
Your line: remember me. The past, made present, at a table. Sixty-five days in.

howItsDone: Nearly all Christians share bread and wine, or grape juice, in memory of the Last Supper, called the Eucharist, Holy Communion, the Lord's Supper, the Mass or the Divine Liturgy. Some churches celebrate it every day or every Sunday, others monthly or a few times a year.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus's last meal, the one in the famous painting.
what it means: a Passover meal where he gives bread and a cup new meaning, and asks his friends to do it again, remembering him.
what a scholar hears: anamnesis, remembrance, echoes Passover's way of making the past present, and Luke alone mentions a cup before the bread as well as after.

notes: Eucharistic theology summaries (Catholic/Orthodox real change; Lutheran real presence 'in, with and under'; Reformed spiritual presence; Baptist memorial) need careful Keeper review for fairness to each church. 'Transubstantiation' is deliberately not used for the Orthodox.
Passover timing: the Synoptics present the supper as a Passover meal; John places it before Passover (John 18:28, 19:14). The myth reveal says so.
Jewish Passover practice of speaking in the first person about the Exodus (Exodus 13:8; the Haggadah 'in every generation') paraphrased. Confirm.
Luke 22:17–20: two cups; verses 19b–20 are absent from a few Western manuscripts. Not discussed.
'The famous painting' in the trapdoor refers to Leonardo's Last Supper; not named.
Hebrew-style doubling ('with desire I have desired') as an intensive; confirm.
